strengths: LPAM addresses a practical stitching problem: repairing local misalignment where an otherwise reasonable seam produces visible artifacts. Its modular, training-free design could benefit existing stitching pipelines.

Tables 1–2 report consistent mean improvements across four seam-cutting methods, five initial alignment methods, and three datasets totaling 79 image pairs. For example, baseline seam SSIM on SEAGULL improves from 0.638 to 0.697.

The pipeline is understandable, with an overview, pseudocode, and qualitative examples showing repaired structures. Ablations examine flow tapering and SSIM window size, while the failure discussion acknowledges the tradeoff between alignment accuracy and smooth reinsertion.
The manuscript links a code repository and explicitly attributes its principal components and borrowed datasets, providing a useful foundation for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation does not adequately establish final mosaic quality. Equations (6–9) measure correspondence around the seam and can miss distortion or discontinuities elsewhere in the modified patches. Table 3 demonstrates this mismatch: untapered flow obtains better RMSE, SSIM, and ZNCC across all three datasets despite introducing boundary artifacts in Figure 3. Dataset-level assessment of boundary quality, geometric preservation, or perceptual preference is needed to validate the central tapering contribution.

Originality and comparative value remain insufficiently established. The contribution combines established SSIM assessment, Otsu thresholding, SIFT-flow, sigmoid weighting, and graph cuts. The related-work discussion itself describes alignment refinement in SEAGULL [22] and dense-flow-based seam/warp estimation in [35], weakening the broad claim that previous approaches only select seams from fixed alignments. Neither quantitative comparisons with these closest approaches nor controls using straightforward seam-band or full-overlap flow refinement establish the advantage of selective patch repair.

The seam acceptance rule in Section 3.2 can classify a uniformly poor seam as plausible: constant positive errors always satisfy max(Q) ≤ 1.5 mean(Q), regardless of their magnitude. This contradicts the stated requirement that every seam pixel have a small error and limits the claimed independence from initial alignment quality. Sensitivity to this gate and to k is not evaluated.

The smooth-consistency claim in Section 3.3 exceeds what the construction establishes. A sigmoid depending on one coordinate does not constrain displacement along every rectangular patch boundary, and fixed graph-cut boundary labels ensure label compatibility rather than continuity of warped image content. The acknowledged failure case is informative, but the reliability of this boundary treatment remains unquantified.

Practical validation is incomplete. The manuscript does not clearly specify alignment-patch padding, overlapping-patch handling, SIFT-flow settings, or image resolutions. Section 4.4 reports roughly 7–10 seconds of additional LPAM processing, often exceeding the host seam-cutting time, without matched timing comparisons against the closest seam-driven alternatives. Consequently, the claimed efficiency advantage is only partially supported.
